question: Has MPSLTD broken decisively into a Stage 4 downtrend after losing its 200-day moving average, and what exact base-building and Stage 2 reclaim signals are required before committing capital?

epigraph.quote: Underwriting Rule: a chart cannot tell you what a business is worth. It can only tell you who is in a hurry, and whether that person is buying or selling.
epigraph.author: Research Desk house maxim

web_blocks.html: The previous seven chapters judged the business and priced its cash flows. Now we inspect the tape, and the verdict is unmistakable: MPS has broken down into a confirmed Stage 4 decline. On our verified 23 November 2026 NSE ledger, MPS closed at ₹2,105.60 (−1.80% on the day, −9.00% over one month, −27.83% over three months), clinging just 1.14% above its 200-day simple moving average (₹2,081.77) and still reading Stage 3 on daily averages [90]. Two sessions later, on the 25 November 2026 live TradingView snapshot, sellers broke the floor cleanly: MPS closed at ₹2,054.80 (−2.41% on the day, −6.17% over one week, −24.56% over three months, −31.02% below its 52-week intraday high of ₹2,979.00) on 23,442 shares—1.47 times its 30-day average volume [91]. Every major weekly and daily moving average now sits above price, confirming a Stage 4 breakdown that blocks new equity capital.

Before reading the levels, recall Stan Weinstein's four-stage rule. Stage analysis uses the 30-week moving average as the primary referee: price above a rising 30-week line marks a Stage 2 advance; price churning sideways around a flattening line marks Stage 1 basing or Stage 3 topping; price sliced below the 30-week line alongside a falling 10-week average marks a Stage 4 decline [92]. Weinstein's core rule for disciplined capital is absolute: never catch a falling Stage 4 knife regardless of how attractive the trailing earnings multiple looks. Wait for selling pressure to exhaust itself, a Stage 1 base to form, and a high-volume Stage 2 reclaim to prove institutions are accumulating again [92]. Our 12 November monograph respected the boundary while MPS still sat 11% above its 200-day average. By 25 November, that last floor gave way.
The moving-average ledger maps every major daily and weekly reference line against both the 23 November verified close and the 25 November live breakdown.

Now it sits 10.4% beneath the 30-week line, 15.4% beneath the falling 50-day line, and 1.4% beneath the broken 200-day line. That is textbook Stage 4 damage.

web_blocks.takeaway: Oversold readings on daily (29.66) and four-hour (27.17) RSI warn that a sharp relief bounce toward ₹2,170 to ₹2,250 can occur at any time, but without a confirmed four-hour upward turn or weekly base, buying oversold Stage 4 breaks destroys capital. MPS is also outside the NSE futures-and-options segment, so no listed options chain exists to structure a defined-risk call spread or hedge.

web_blocks.html: We also reconcile a crucial scanner quirk before mapping support and resistance levels. Because MPS sliced below its 200-day moving average and monthly pivot S1, TradingView's automated scanner falls back to broken overhead moving averages—printing a raw support zone of ₹2,275.33 to ₹2,464.37 and an invalidation stop of ₹2,244.41. Every one of those numbers sits above the live ₹2,054.80 price! We never publish a stop-loss above current market price or treat broken resistance as support. Instead, the price map below distinguishes broken overhead supply from lower passive Stage 4 reference shelves.

web_blocks.takeaway: MPS has surrendered 56.0% of its entire March–August 2026 advance (52.8% at the 23 November ledger close). With TradingView's raw levels sitting 10% to 20% overhead as resistance, our passive ₹1,810 to ₹1,920 reference band and ₹1,750 floor sit cleanly below market price—explicitly flagged as monitor-only markers while zero capital is deployed.

web_blocks.html: Volume behavior and institutional ownership explain why MPS breaks sharply once bids step back. The ledger counted 9 distribution days in 25 sessions through 23 November, followed by a 23,442-share breakdown bar (1.47x 30-day average) on 25 November [90, 91]. With promoters holding 68.34% and free float worth roughly ₹1,113 Cr at ₹2,054.80, average daily turnover of ₹3 Cr to ₹4 Cr creates air pockets whenever sellers press.

web_blocks.caption: Free-float ownership across recent quarters (promoter stake steady at 68.34% via ADI BPO Services)
web_blocks.takeaway: Combined institutional ownership (FII + DII) sits at just 3.60% of total equity, down from 4.27% in December 2023 [93]. Without a large institutional sponsor defending support, a retail-heavy 27.3% float produces rapid overshoots once the 200-day average gives way. We will watch the December 2026 shareholding filing to see whether domestic funds step in or exit.

web_blocks.html: Relative strength confirms that opportunity cost is working against MPS. On the 23 November verified NSE ledger, MPS trailed the Nifty 50 by −29.66% over 28 sessions and −32.44% over 63 sessions while the broader Indian market remained in an uptrend with narrow breadth (55.2% of Nifty 500 stocks above 50DMA, 3 Nifty distribution days, 7 of 11 sectors above 20/50/200 DMA) [90]. web_blocks.takeaway: MPS has lost its relative-strength leadership. Over the past three months, MPS (−24.6%) fell identically to Stage 4 peer eClerx (−24.5%) and worse than Newgen (−21.2%), while Stage 2 services peers Firstsource (+6.6%) and Cyient (+10.2%) held above their 30-week averages [91].

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Why we cancel a watch when the floor breaks
paragraphs: Two weeks ago our plan looked neat on paper: wait for ₹2,070 at the rising 200-day average and buy a starter with a ₹2,005 stop. Today the stock reached ₹2,055—and instead of rushing to fill that old plan, we are rejecting it. That reversal is the heart of disciplined underwriting.

When price reaches your old support zone on 1.47x down-volume, slices cleanly beneath the 200-day average and pivot S1, and arrives alongside freshly uncovered Pass 1 cracks in organic Education and Unbound's Johns Hopkins licensor, the original thesis for a counter-trend bounce is void. You do not hold onto an old limit order after the floor gives way.

web_blocks.takeaway: There is no shortcut back into MPS. A falling Stage 4 chart demands two distinct technical proofs—a completed Stage 1 base followed by a high-volume Stage 2 reclaim above the 30-week average—paired with H2 FY27 fundamental evidence.

web_blocks.html: Technical re-underwriting gate. Remove the Stage 4 rejection only after MPS completes a multi-week Stage 1 base and prints a decisive weekly close above the 30-week moving average (currently ₹2,292.98) with the 10-week EMA turning upward on at least 2x average weekly volume (above ~32,000 shares per day). Until that reclaim occurs—and until Pass 1's H2 organic Education and Research billing checks pass—maintain zero allocation and ignore oversold intraday bounces.

Chapter 9 pulls Chapters 1 through 8 together into a unified, unbiased verdict across Bull, Bear, and three investment horizons, detailing our zero-allocation posture, monitor-only alerts, and where marginal Zerodha INR cash belongs instead.

book_paragraphs: Two weeks ago, MPS stood on a knife-edge. At ₹2,297 it was wobbling on its thirty-week moving average while still resting eleven per cent above its rising 200-day average. That gave a patient investor a logical thought: let it pull back to the 200-day line near ₹2,070 and see if buyers defend it. Between 12 November and 25 November, the market answered that test—and the buyers failed to show up.

Look at the two closes that bracket this refresh. On our verified 23 November NSE ledger, MPS settled at ₹2,105.60, clinging by just one per cent above its 200-day moving average of ₹2,082 after chalking up nine distribution days in twenty-five sessions. Two sessions later, on 25 November, sellers pushed the stock straight through both the 200-day average and monthly pivot support at ₹2,066, closing at ₹2,054.80 on 23,442 shares—nearly one and a half times normal thirty-day volume. In Stan Weinstein's framework, that move removes all ambiguity. MPS is no longer hovering on a Stage 3 boundary. It is in a confirmed Stage 4 decline.

Every moving average that institutional trend followers respect now sits overhead as resistance. Price trades more than ten per cent beneath its thirty-week moving average at ₹2,293, eleven per cent beneath its falling ten-week exponential average at ₹2,310, and more than fifteen per cent beneath a rapidly declining fifty-day average at ₹2,428. Even the four-hour chart offers zero sign of stabilisation: four-hour RSI sits at 27, daily RSI sits just under 30, and price trails its four-hour twenty-period average by more than five per cent. Yes, readings that stretched can spark a violent short-term bounce toward ₹2,200—but in Stage 4, oversold bounces are traps that hand shares from impatient sellers to hopeful dip-buyers.

One mechanical detail is worth pointing out clearly. Because MPS fell beneath its last major support floor, automated scanner software falls back to broken overhead moving averages and prints a support band of ₹2,275 to ₹2,464 with a stop at ₹2,244—all well above today's price. Obviously you never treat overhead resistance as support or place a stop above the current quote. Below ₹2,055, the next true technical reference shelves lie at the 61.8 per cent retracement near ₹1,964, monthly pivot S2 at ₹1,811, and ultimately the March 2026 base around ₹1,336 to ₹1,393. We mark ₹1,810 to ₹1,920 with a ₹1,750 reference floor strictly as passive observation benchmarks—not as live buy orders.

Who is on the other side of this tape? Promoters own 68.34 per cent and do not trade, while foreign and domestic institutions together own just 3.60 per cent of the company. That leaves more than twenty-seven per cent of the shares in the hands of roughly 26,300 public retail holders, trading only three to four crore rupees on an average day. Thin retail-dominated order books overshoot dramatically in both directions—just as MPS fell 52 per cent into March 2026 and then doubled in five months into August. And because MPS is not part of the NSE futures-and-options segment, there is no listed options market to cushion volatility with defined-risk spreads.

Relative strength seals the timing case. Over the past three months, MPS lagged the Nifty 50 by over 32 percentage points while dropping 24.6 per cent—matching Stage 4 peer eClerx while Stage 2 peers such as Firstsource and Cyient stayed positive above their thirty-week lines. Meanwhile, Indian equity markets remain in a selective uptrend with plenty of confirmed Stage 2 leaders available. Catching a falling Stage 4 knife when both the tape and Pass 1's organic Education and Unbound findings flash warning lights is a mistake we refuse to make.

book_callouts.quote: Broken support becomes overhead supply; never mistake an overhead moving average for a buy zone.
book_callouts.text: When a stock slices beneath its 200-day average and monthly pivot S1, automated technical scanners can point upward to broken moving averages. Reconciling those numbers explicitly prevents bad execution.

book_subsections.title: What a real Stage 1 base and Stage 2 reclaim look like
paragraphs: Investors often ask how to know when a Stage 4 decline has actually ended. The answer is never a single green candle or a low RSI print. First, the stock must stop making lower lows for several weeks—building a sideways Stage 1 base where daily price swings tighten and trading volume dries up to half of normal levels, proving panicked sellers have run out of shares.

Second, price must punch back above its thirty-week moving average—currently near ₹2,293—on a Friday weekly close accompanied by at least twice normal weekly volume, while the ten-week average curls upward. Only when that technical repair aligns with second-half fundamental proof in Education and Research billing will we re-open the MPS file. Missing the bottom ten per cent of a turnaround is a small insurance premium for avoiding another fifty-per-cent drawdown.
